opening_note: November is when San Diego's evenings finally turn. The days still reach the high sixties, but the nights drop into the fifties, and for the first time since spring an hour with a pot in the oven sounds good. The first satsumas arrive, persimmons ripen on bare trees, and the cool-weather vegetables come back — leeks, fennel, chard, cauliflower. Everything below comes from one store and a fish market, and it all keeps you cooking through the week.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

bring_home.cost_note: A week like the one suggested runs about $90–135 at a well-stocked supermarket and a fish market, depending mostly on the fish: halibut is the treat, rockfish or lingcod keep it near the low end. The first week adds about $15 for Parmesan, cinnamon, and brown sugar that last the month. Everything in this edition is on these lines — nothing else to buy.

month_card.sub: The first cool nights, and the first citrus.

field_notes.name: Squat ones are for now.
field_notes.body: There are two persimmons in the bin, and they're eaten differently. A squat, flat-bottomed Fuyu is never astringent: eat it crisp, like an apple. A pointed, acorn-shaped Hachiya is full of tannin until it's completely soft — so soft it feels like a water balloon — and one bite early will dry out your whole mouth. Buy Fuyus to eat this week; buy Hachiyas only if you can wait.

field_notes.name: A loose peel is a good sign.
field_notes.body: Satsumas grow a puffy peel that comes away from the fruit; that's the variety, not age. Judge them by weight instead: pick up two of the same size and buy the heavier one. They're the reason to keep a bag in the fridge through December.

field_notes.name: A braise is a sear that keeps going.
field_notes.body: Everything October taught about the sear — dry meat, hot pan, hands off until it lets go — is the first step of a braise. Then add a little liquid, partway up, and give it a low oven and time. Leave the lid off if there's skin to keep crisp. In December, the same pot holds a pork shoulder for three hours; the steps don't change.

field_notes.name: Chard stems go in first.
field_notes.body: A bunch of chard is two vegetables: stems that need five minutes and leaves that need one. Chop the stems and start them with the leeks or the garlic; tear in the leaves at the end. Thrown in together, you get stringy stems or gray leaves.

drink.name: Sherman Heights Café de Olla
drink.intro: One drink. The evenings turned, and November opens with Día de los Muertos.
drink.card_line: Coffee, cinnamon, brown sugar, satsuma peel
drink.method: Bring four cups of water to a simmer in a saucepan with the cinnamon stick, brown sugar, and satsuma peel, and let it bubble gently for five minutes so the cinnamon opens up. Take it off the heat, stir in a third of a cup of ground coffee, and let it steep for four minutes. Pour it through a fine strainer, or a paper filter if you want it clean. It should taste like coffee first, then spice, and only a little sweet. It's traditionally made in a clay pot, the olla; any saucepan works.

try_another_way.context: Start with two tablespoons if you take your coffee black.
A heaped half cup of coffee instead of a third, for slow mornings.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: A braise should barely move.
one_thing_to_notice.body: Open the oven and look at the pot. The liquid around the chicken should be shivering — a few lazy bubbles at the edges — not boiling. A hard boil tightens the meat and clouds the sauce. If it's rolling, turn the oven down twenty-five degrees. The same goes for the soup on the stove.

satsumas.name: Satsuma mandarins
satsumas.tile_uses: The jar, the weekend braise, mornings, the drink
satsumas.why_now: Satsumas are among the first California citrus of the season, and they start arriving in November — sweet, seedless, and so loose in their skins they peel in one piece. They're at their best now and through December.
how_to_choose: Heavy for their size; light ones have started to dry out
A puffy, loose peel is normal for a satsuma, not a sign of age
Bright orange, with a little green near the stem still fine
No soft, sunken spots
satsumas.buy_this_much: A 2-lb bag, about ten. One goes into the jar and the braise; the rest get eaten out of hand.
satsumas.price_note: Usually sold in bags or by the pound; the bags are cheaper and just as good.

fuyu-persimmons.tile_uses: The halibut salad, mornings, a snack
fuyu-persimmons.why_now: Persimmons ripen on bare trees in November, and San Diego County grows them. Fuyus are the squat, tomato-shaped kind you can eat crisp like an apple — sweet, a little like honey and pumpkin.
how_to_choose: Squat and flat-bottomed: that's a Fuyu, ready to eat firm
Deep orange all over, with no yellow-green patches
Firm but not rock-hard for salads; a little give for eating out of hand
Skip pointed, acorn-shaped ones unless they're jelly-soft: those are Hachiya

fuyu-persimmons.price_note: Sold by the each. Farmers markets often have them in bags for less.

fuyu-persimmons.one_thing_to_learn: Shape tells you how to eat a persimmon. A squat Fuyu is never astringent and can be eaten crisp. A pointed Hachiya is full of tannin until it's completely soft, like a water balloon; bite one early and your mouth goes dry.

fennel.name: Fennel
fennel.tile_uses: The jar, the weekend braise, the halibut salad
fennel.why_now: Fennel is a cool-weather vegetable; as the nights drop into the fifties it comes back sweet and crisp. Raw, it's anise-cool and crunchy; cooked slowly, it turns soft and mild.
how_to_choose: Heavy, tight, white bulbs
No brown bruising or splitting on the outer layers

chicken-thighs.name: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs
chicken-thighs.tile_uses: The weekend braise, the roast chicken and cauliflower
chicken-thighs.why_now: There's nothing seasonal about chicken. What changes in November is the weather: the first cool evenings make an hour-long braise appealing again, and bone-in, skin-on thighs are the cut built for it. This is the month's cut.
how_to_choose: Skin that covers the whole thigh, not shrunken back
Pink, plump meat with no gray edges
No liquid pooling in the package
Similar-sized thighs, so they cook evenly
chicken-thighs.buy_this_much: About 2½–3 lbs (6 thighs) for the braise, and 4 thighs for the roast pan.
chicken-thighs.price_note: Bone-in, skin-on thighs are one of the cheapest cuts in the case, well below boneless.

chicken-thighs.one_thing_to_learn: Thighs are done at 165°F but better at 175–195°F: dark meat has connective tissue that keeps softening as it cooks, so a braised thigh at 195°F is more tender than one pulled at 165°F, not less.
